You see, I had stowed my handkerchief in my helmet, along with a few other things. But this was the kind of helmet you couldn't remove without help. That hadn't crossed my mind when I put it there; in fact, I hadn't known. I'd imagined it would be an especially convenient place. Now the thought of it sitting there, so close and apparently handy, yet completely beyond my reach, made everything worse. Yes, what you chiefly want is whatever you can't have; everyone has noticed that. Well, it drove every other thought from my mind and concentrated all my attention inside that helmet. Mile after mile, my thoughts stayed there, imagining the handkerchief, seeing it before me. All the while salty sweat kept running into my eyes, and the cloth I needed was out of reach. It was bitterly frustrating. Written down, this sounds trivial, but it was nothing of the sort. It was misery in its most substantial form. I wouldn't say so if it weren't true. I decided that next time I would bring a handbag, however it looked and whatever anyone said. Naturally those metal-clad dandies of the Round Table would consider it outrageous, and might raise hell over it. But I wanted comfort first; fashion could wait. We jogged along, occasionally crossing a dusty patch that rose in clouds, filled my nose, and made me sneeze and weep. Of course I said things I shouldn't have. I won't deny it. I'm no better than anyone else.

We seemed unable to meet a soul in this deserted Britain, not even an ogre. Considering my mood, that was fortunate for the ogre—particularly an ogre carrying a handkerchief. Most knights would have concentrated on taking his armor. As far as I was concerned, provided I got his bandanna, he could keep every piece of his hardware.

Meanwhile it was growing steadily hotter inside my suit. The sun kept beating down, heating the iron more and more. When you're hot like that, every small thing gets on your nerves. At a trot I rattled like a crate full of plates, which irritated me. Worse still, I could hardly bear the shield flapping and banging, first against my chest and then around my back. If I slowed to a walk, the joints of my armor creaked and shrieked with that maddening wheelbarrow sound. At that speed we made no breeze, so I was in danger of frying inside the stove. Besides, the more gently you moved, the more heavily the iron pressed down, until you seemed to gain several tons every minute.

She would make such a delightful companion for Emma.”

Mr. Woodhouse agreed with everything, but added,

“Our young friend Harriet Smith, though, is another pretty young person of just that sort. You'll like Harriet. Emma couldn't have a better companion.”

“I'm very glad to hear it. Only, we know Jane Fairfax to be so exceptionally accomplished and admirable! And she's precisely Emma's age.”

They discussed this subject with great satisfaction, then moved to others of equal importance and equal harmony. Still, the evening was not to end without another brief disturbance. The gruel arrived, furnishing plenty of conversation: generous praise, numerous observations, absolute certainty that it benefited every constitution, and rather fierce attacks on the many households where it was never served in an acceptable state. Unfortunately, among the failures his daughter could describe, the most recent—and therefore foremost in her thoughts—was her own cook at South End. This young woman, hired for their stay, had never understood what she meant by a bowl of nice, smooth gruel, thin but not excessively thin. However often she asked for it and gave her instructions, she never received anything tolerable. This offered a dangerous opening.

“Ah!” said Mr. Woodhouse, shaking his head and gazing at her with affectionate anxiety. To Emma, that exclamation meant, “Ah! The unfortunate consequences of your going to South End are endless. It cannot bear discussion.” For a little while she hoped he would indeed leave it undiscussed, and that some silent reflection would be enough to restore his enjoyment of his own smooth gruel. After several minutes, however, he began:

“I shall always regret your going to the seaside this autumn instead of coming here.”

“But why should you regret it, sir? I assure you, the children benefited enormously.”

“And if you absolutely had to go to the seaside, you should at least have chosen somewhere other than South End. South End is unhealthy. Perry was surprised to hear you had settled on it.”

“I know many people think so, but they're quite mistaken, sir. We were all perfectly healthy there, and the mud never caused us the slightest trouble. Mr. Wingfield says the belief that it's unhealthy is entirely wrong. I'm sure we can trust his opinion, because he thoroughly understands the character of the air, and his own brother and family have visited repeatedly.”

“You should have chosen Cromer, my dear, if you were going anywhere. Perry once spent a week there, and he considers it the finest of all the places for sea bathing.

Many American women, on leaving their own country, acquire an air of permanent poor health, believing it to be a sign of European sophistication. Mrs. Otis had never made that mistake. She possessed a superb constitution and an astonishing supply of natural vitality. In many ways, indeed, she was thoroughly English: an excellent illustration of how much we now share with America—everything, of course, except the language. Her eldest son was Washington, so named during a burst of parental patriotism that he never stopped regretting. He was a fair-haired, reasonably handsome young man whose qualifications for American diplomacy consisted of leading the German dance at the Newport Casino for three consecutive seasons. Even in London, he enjoyed a reputation as an excellent dancer. His only weaknesses were gardenias and the aristocracy; in every other respect he was extremely sensible. Miss Virginia E. Otis was a small girl of fifteen, graceful and lovely as a fawn, with a splendid independence in her large blue eyes. She was a remarkable horsewoman. Once, on her pony, she had raced old Lord Bilton twice around the park, beating him by a length and a half just before the statue of Achilles. The young Duke of Cheshire was so delighted that he proposed to her immediately. His guardians sent him back to Eton that very evening, weeping bitterly. Next came the twins, generally known as “The Stars and Stripes” because they were forever being whipped. They were charming boys and, apart from the worthy Minister, the family's only genuine republicans.

Since Canterville Chase lay seven miles from Ascot, the closest railway station, Mr. Otis had wired ahead for an open carriage to collect them. They began their drive in excellent spirits. It was a beautiful July evening, and a delicate fragrance from the pine woods filled the air. Occasionally they heard a wood pigeon dwelling lovingly on its own sweet song, or glimpsed a pheasant's gleaming breast deep among the rustling ferns. Small squirrels watched from the beech trees as they passed. Rabbits darted through the undergrowth and over moss-covered rises, their white tails lifted. But as they turned into the avenue leading to Canterville Chase, clouds suddenly covered the sky. An odd stillness seemed to grip the air. A great flock of rooks flew silently overhead, and before they reached the house, several large raindrops had begun to fall.

An elderly woman waited on the steps to welcome them, tidily dressed in black silk with a white apron and cap.
